title: Hungary waits for the January price resets before easing
summary: Hungary’s Monetary Council held the base rate at 6.50% on 27 January. It expected inflation to fall briefly below its 3% target early in 2026, then rise close to the top of the tolerance band before settling sustainably at target in the second half of 2027. That sequence explains why the first low reading would have little power on its own to unlock a cut. Two nearer-term tests mattered more to the Council: how firms reset prices at the beginning of the year, and whether financial markets remained stable enough for households’ inflation expectations to move towards target. The decision table shows the entire interest-rate corridor held steady with effect from 28 January: overnight deposits at 5.50%, collateralised overnight loans at 7.50%.

The recent price data contained evidence on both sides. Headline inflation ended December at 3.3%, below the 4.4% average for 2025. Those figures cover different periods: the change from one to the other is not a monthly disinflation rate. Core inflation remained higher than the December headline rate, at 3.8%. The Council traced much of the recent improvement to fuel and processed food. At the same time, observed price resets in market services and tradable goods exceeded historical averages. A business can report subdued expectations for future price increases while raising its own prices more than usual during a particular reset window. Household inflation expectations, meanwhile, had stopped falling. These differences underpin the Council’s caution about extrapolating from the aggregate index (release, paragraphs beginning “In December 2025” and “The general improvement”).

The forint matters twice in this account. Its appreciation was already working through to procurement prices, reinforcing a generally better external cost environment. Separately, the Council viewed exchange-market stability as important for anchoring household expectations. A change in the currency could therefore alter both the cost of inputs and how the public interprets the likely persistence of price changes. Maintaining a positive real interest rate was part of the strategy for preserving that stability. The release gives neither an exchange-rate threshold nor the expected inflation measure used to judge the real stance. Subtracting one month’s headline inflation mechanically from the base rate would miss the forward-looking element of the argument (inflation outlook and monetary policy paragraphs).

Domestic activity gave the Council competing reasons to wait. Retail sales were expanding but industrial and construction output had contracted in November. Labour-market tightness had eased over several quarters while unemployment remained historically low. The projected improvement in domestic growth depends on higher real wages and government measures supporting household income, with consumption contributing throughout the forecast horizon. For industry, the mechanism is different: a recovery in export markets would allow capacity added by earlier investment projects to translate into higher industrial exports. Weak industrial production today and stronger projected consumption thus describe different exposures within the economy. The Council also expects a current account surplus averaging around 2% of GDP. It identifies a fiscal trade-off: higher public spending can support demand while making a reduction in the debt ratio harder (paragraphs on the real economy and the growth outlook).

The international setting offers limited protection against a reversal of the favourable cost and currency trends. Oil and gas prices had risen significantly, and risk indicators remained sensitive to trade and geopolitical developments. The release attributes two possible Fed cuts in 2026 to market pricing and an unchanged ECB rate to market expectations. These are descriptions of what investors expected abroad, not forecasts for Hungarian policy or evidence of what was priced into Hungarian rates. The Council judged the risks around its inflation projection balanced, yet still saw a need for tight monetary conditions: a balanced distribution around a path that takes until late 2027 to deliver sustained price stability can warrant patience. For a portfolio manager, the most informative near-term evidence in this statement would be a combination of restrained price resets, renewed improvement in household expectations and an orderly currency. The Council supplies no timetable for easing or market-price reference against which to measure a surprise.

questions.question: How much of the January price reset reflects persistent domestic cost pressure?
questions.detail: The Council identifies above-average repricing in services and tradables while attributing much of the recent headline relief to fuel and processed food. It does not quantify how many firms raised prices or how large their increases were. That distinction matters for the timing of the first cut. Compare the distribution of January price changes with earlier reset seasons using detailed consumer-price releases and the MNB’s inflation analysis; examine breadth separately from the largest individual changes.

questions.question: Is forint appreciation reaching household expectations as well as firms’ input costs?
questions.detail: The release points to procurement-price relief, while household expectations stagnated. If consumers respond chiefly to salient food or energy prices, the influence of a stable currency on expectations could arrive later than the effect on import costs. Look for successive MNB household and corporate survey releases alongside import-price and retail components, using consistent horizons. A widening gap would complicate the case for easing even with a favourable headline print.

questions.question: Can stronger consumption and an improving external balance coexist on the projected path?
questions.detail: Household income measures should support consumption, while earlier investment should raise export capacity. The release does not specify how quickly external orders will use that capacity or how import-intensive additional consumption will be. Use the central bank’s expenditure forecasts, trade data and the government’s fiscal releases to assess which leg of the projection bears more risk. That balance matters for both forint exposure and the duration of restrictive rates.
